title: ROS 2 Computational Graph (Nodes, Executors, Topics, Services, Actions, QoS), TF2 Frames, URDF & ros2_control

blocks.x: This is the dedicated **ROS 2 bridge module** before Step 2.7 (`06-robotics.T2.07`) and your gateway to the Graduate Goal (building and tuning a custom robot arm with ROS 2 and a learned policy). Before running Cartesian impedance controllers (`06-robotics.T2.07`), `MoveIt 2`, or `Hugging Face LeRobot` policies (`06-robotics.T3.07`), you must master the complete **ROS 2 (`Jazzy` / `Lyrical`)** architecture: how **Nodes** and **Executors** (`SingleThreadedExecutor` vs. `MultiThreadedExecutor` + `CallbackGroups`) schedule callbacks, how **Topics**, **Services**, **Actions**, and **Parameters** exchange typed messages under strict **QoS** rules (`Reliable` vs. `Best-Effort`, `Transient Local` vs. `Volatile`), how workspaces are built (`package.xml`, `colcon build`, Python `LaunchDescription`), how the **`tf2` transform tree** chains 3D coordinate frames (`world -> base_link -> link_1 -> tool0`) from your **URDF/Xacro** robot description, and how **`ros2_control`** separates real-time hardware drivers (`SystemInterface::read()` / `write()`) from controllers (`joint_trajectory_controller`) without DDS network jitter! Already know this? Take the Skip test in section 7 first.

blocks.caption: Boxes are processes and arrows are typed messages; nothing calls anything directly.
An executor is a deadline: the work has to finish before the next callback.

blocks.x: Imagine a robot software stack as a modern airport:

items.x: **ROS 2 Nodes, Executors & Callback Groups:** Each **Node** (`rclcpp::Node` / `rclpy.node.Node`) is a modular specialist team (Camera Node, Planner Node, Safety Monitor Node). An **Executor** is the dispatcher that pulls incoming events (timers, topic messages, service requests) from the DDS middleware queue and runs your callback functions. A `SingleThreadedExecutor` runs one callback at a time sequentially (if one callback blocks for $200\text{ ms}$, every timer in that node stalls!), whereas a `MultiThreadedExecutor` paired with `MutuallyExclusiveCallbackGroup` or `ReentrantCallbackGroup` lets a slow planning service run on Thread B without delaying a $100\text{ Hz}$ state-publishing timer on Thread A.
**Topics, Services, Actions & Parameters:**

**Topics (Publish / Subscribe):** Continuous radio broadcast streams (`sensor_msgs/msg/JointState`, `geometry_msgs/msg/Twist`) governed by **Quality of Service (QoS)**: high-rate camera/IMU streams use `Best-Effort / Volatile / KeepLast(1)` (drop an old frame rather than stall on a retry), whereas latched maps and robot descriptions (`/robot_description`) use `Reliable / Transient Local`.
**Services (`srv`):** Fast synchronous request-reply calls (`std_srvs/srv/SetBool` to zero a force sensor—never use for long blocking motions!).

**Actions (`action`):** Long-running preemptible state machines (`control_msgs/action/FollowJointTrajectory`) consisting of a **Goal** request, a continuous **Feedback** stream (percent complete / tracking error), a final **Result**, and mid-flight **Cancel** support.

**Parameters & Launch Files:** Dynamic node settings (`kp`, `max_vel`, `urdf_path`) loaded at startup from YAML via a Python `LaunchDescription` (`ros2 launch my_arm_bringup arm.launch.py`) after building the workspace with `colcon build --symlink-install`.

**`tf2` & URDF/Xacro:** The airport's live 3D radar map. Your **URDF** file declares each `<link>` (`<inertial>`, `<visual>`, `<collision>`) and `<joint>` (`parent`, `child`, `<origin xyz rpy>`, `<axis xyz>`). The `robot_state_publisher` node reads the URDF plus `/joint_states` and broadcasts the $SE(3)$ transform tree onto `/tf` (dynamic joints) and `/tf_static` (rigidly bolted sensors) so any node can ask "Where is `camera_optical_frame` relative to `tool0` at timestamp $t$?"

**`ros2_control` (`controller_manager`):** The hard-real-time engine room. Instead of sending $1\text{ kHz}$ motor torques over network topics, `ros2_control` loads your C++ controller plugin and your C++ hardware driver (`SystemInterface::read(time, period)` $\to$ `update(time, period)` $\to$ `write(time, period)`) into the **same real-time process**, passing raw C++ pointers to `state_interfaces` (`position`, `velocity`, `effort`) and `command_interfaces` (`effort`, `position`) with zero serialization jitter!
**ROS 2 Graph, Executor Scheduling & QoS Compatibility Rule:**

**QoS `offered >= requested` Rule:** A publisher offering `(Reliability_pub, Durability_pub)` and a subscriber requesting `(Reliability_sub, Durability_sub)` connect iff **both** policies are compatible:

blocks.x: where $\text{Reliable (1)} > \text{Best-Effort (0)}$ and $\text{Transient Local (1)} > \text{Volatile (0)}$. A `Best-Effort` publisher **cannot** connect to a `Reliable` subscriber, and a `Volatile` publisher **cannot** connect to a `Transient Local` subscriber!

items.x: **Topic Bandwidth & Executor Budget:** Publishing messages of size $B_{\text{msg}}$ bytes at frequency $f_{\text{pub}}$ ($\text{Hz}$) to $N_{\text{sub}}$ unicast subscribers consumes network bandwidth $R_{\text{MB/s}} = \frac{N_{\text{sub}} \cdot B_{\text{msg}} \cdot f_{\text{pub}}}{10^6}\text{ MB/s}$. In a `SingleThreadedExecutor`, the worst-case blocking delay before a high-priority timer callback can fire is the maximum execution time $\max_k C_k$ of any callback in that executor.

**`tf2` Tree Structure & $SE(3)$ Frame Lookup:** Every `tf2` coordinate frame has **at most one parent** (forming a directed tree with $N - 1$ directed edges for $N$ frames, never a cycle or multi-parent diamond). Given chain `base_link` $\xrightarrow{T_{b1}(q_1)}$ `link_1` $\xrightarrow{T_{12}(q_2)}$ `tool0`, `tf2` computes the transform from `tool0` to `base_link` at timestamp $t$ via:

blocks.tex: T_{\text{base}\leftarrow\text{tool0}}(t) = T_{b1}(q_1(t)) \cdot T_{12}(q_2(t)), \quad p_{\text{base}}(t) = T_{\text{base}\leftarrow\text{tool0}}(t) \, p_{\text{tool0}}

blocks.x: For a revolute URDF joint with origin offset $p_{\text{xyz}}$ and unit axis $\hat{a} = [0, 0, 1]^\top$, $T_{\text{parent}\leftarrow\text{child}}(q) = \begin{bmatrix} R_z(q) & p_{\text{xyz}} \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$. When querying `lookupTransform(target, source, t_sensor)` between asynchronous streams, `tf2` linearly/SLERP interpolates between buffered timestamps $t_a \le t_{\text{sensor}} \le t_b$:

items.x: **Quaternion Orientation & SLERP in `tf2`:** Each frame's rotation is buffered as a **unit quaternion** $q = (w, x, y, z)$, and an orientation query interpolates the rotation with **SLERP**, not a linear blend:

blocks.x: Because $q$ and $-q$ are the same attitude, `tf2` negates $q_b$ when $q_a \cdot q_b < 0$ so the interpolation takes the short arc; blending the four components linearly shortens the quaternion, and renormalizing it does not restore constant angular speed between the samples.

items.x: **`ros2_control` Lifecycle & Real-Time `read -> update -> write` Loop:** Inside `controller_manager` running on a `SCHED_FIFO` real-time thread at period $\Delta t = 1/f_{\text{ctrl}}$ ($\text{s}$):

**Step A (`read`):** `hardware_interface::SystemInterface::read(time, period)` unpacks encoder/current feedback from SocketCAN (`04-embedded.T2.05`) or `micro-ROS` into exported `state_interfaces` $(q_i, \dot{q}_i, \tau_{i,\text{meas}})$.
**Step B (`update`):** Active controllers (`JointTrajectoryController`, Cartesian impedance) execute `update(time, period)` in-memory and write `command_interfaces` $(\tau_{i,\text{cmd}})$.

**Step C (`write`):** `SystemInterface::write(time, period)` packs $\tau_{i,\text{cmd}}$ into CAN-FD MIT frames and transmits them to the actuators, satisfying $t_{\text{read}} + t_{\text{update}} + t_{\text{write}} \le \Delta t$.

blocks.x: **Predict first (before you run it):** Commit to three outcomes before the code runs. (1) Of the $16$ QoS `(Reliability, Durability)` combinations, how many connect under `offered >= requested`, and does `Best-Effort` into `Reliable` connect? (2) With $q_1 = 0$ and $q_2 = \pi/2$, where does $p_{\text{in,tool}} = [0.15, 0.0, 0.0, 1]^\top$ land in `base_link`? (3) Between $t_a = 1.000\text{ s}$ ($x = 0.20\text{ m}$) and $t_b = 1.010\text{ s}$ ($x = 0.25\text{ m}$), what does `tf2` return at $t = 1.004\text{ s}$? Two tells: a count of $16$ means you tested equality instead of $\ge$, so the two failing rows went unnoticed; a point that lands at $[0.25, -0.15, 0.10]$ means the joint turned backwards, and an interpolated value that equals either endpoint means $\alpha$ was divided by the wrong interval.

Simulate a complete ROS 2 + `tf2` + `ros2_control` pipeline in pure Python: (1) verify the full 2D QoS `(Reliability, Durability)` compatibility matrix and compute camera topic bandwidth, (2) run `robot_state_publisher` forward kinematics and `tf2` temporal interpolation on a 2-DOF URDF chain (`base_link -> link_1 -> tool0`), and (3) execute one $1\text{ kHz}$ `ros2_control` `read() -> update() -> write()` tick.

import math

def qos_compatible(pub_rel: bool, pub_trans_local: bool, sub_rel: bool, sub_trans_local: bool) -> bool:
    # Offered >= Requested for both Reliability (Reliable=True > BestEffort=False)
    # and Durability (TransientLocal=True > Volatile=False)
    rel_ok = int(pub_rel) >= int(sub_rel)
    dur_ok = int(pub_trans_local) >= int(sub_trans_local)
    return rel_ok and dur_ok

assert qos_compatible(True, True, True, True) is True
assert qos_compatible(True, False, False, False) is True
assert qos_compatible(False, False, True, False) is False  # Best-Effort pub -> Reliable sub FAILS!
assert qos_compatible(True, False, True, True) is False    # Volatile pub -> TransientLocal sub FAILS!

def urdf_revolute_z(xyz: tuple[float, float, float], q_rad: float) -> list[list[float]]:
    c, s = math.cos(q_rad), math.sin(q_rad)
    return [[c, -s, 0.0, xyz[0]],
            [s,  c, 0.0, xyz[1]],
            [0.0, 0.0, 1.0, xyz[2]],
            [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0]]

def mat4_mul(A: list[list[float]], B: list[list[float]]) -> list[list[float]]:
    return [[sum(A[i][k] * B[k][j] for k in range(4)) for j in range(4)] for i in range(4)]

# TF2 chain: base_link --(joint1 at [0,0,0.1], q1=0)--> link_1 --(joint2 at [0.25,0,0], q2=pi/2)--> tool0
T_b_l1 = urdf_revolute_z((0.0, 0.0, 0.10), q_rad=0.0)
T_l1_tool = urdf_revolute_z((0.25, 0.0, 0.0), q_rad=math.pi / 2.0)
T_b_tool = mat4_mul(T_b_l1, T_l1_tool)
p_in_tool = [0.15, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0]  # 15 cm along tool0 +X
p_in_base = [sum(T_b_tool[i][j] * p_in_tool[j] for j in range(4)) for i in range(3)]
assert all(math.isclose(p_in_base[i], [0.25, 0.15, 0.10][i], abs_tol=1e-9) for i in range(3))

# tf2 buffer interpolation between t_a = 1.000 s (x = 0.20 m) and t_b = 1.010 s (x = 0.25 m) at t_query = 1.004 s:
alpha = (1.004 - 1.000) / (1.010 - 1.000)
x_interp = (1.0 - alpha) * 0.20 + alpha * 0.25
assert math.isclose(x_interp, 0.22, rel_tol=1e-9)

# ros2_control 1 kHz cycle: read() -> controller.update() -> write()
state_if = {"q": 0.0, "dq": 0.0}
cmd_if = {"effort": 0.0}
def hw_read(can_q: float, can_dq: float) -> None:
    state_if["q"], state_if["dq"] = can_q, can_dq
def controller_update(q_des: float, kp: float = 20.0, kd: float = 1.5) -> None:
    cmd_if["effort"] = kp * (q_des - state_if["q"]) - kd * state_if["dq"]

hw_read(can_q=0.40, can_dq=0.20)
controller_update(q_des=0.50)
assert math.isclose(cmd_if["effort"], 20.0 * 0.10 - 1.5 * 0.20, rel_tol=1e-9)
print(f"p_in_base={[round(x, 4) for x in p_in_base]}, x_tf2={x_interp:.3f} m, effort_cmd={cmd_if['effort']:.2f} N*m")

blocks.x: In the `tf2` tree above (`T_b_l1 = urdf_revolute_z((0, 0, 0.10), q1)` and `T_l1_tool = urdf_revolute_z((0.25, 0, 0), q2)`), compute (a) the 3D position of `p_in_tool = [0.15, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0]` in `base_link` when $q_1 = \pi/2\text{ rad}$ and $q_2 = 0.0\text{ rad}$, and (b) the interpolated `tf2` joint angle $q(t_{\text{query}})$ at $t_{\text{query}} = 2.006\text{ s}$ between buffered samples $(t_a = 2.000\text{ s}, q_a = 0.50\text{ rad})$ and $(t_b = 2.010\text{ s}, q_b = 0.70\text{ rad})$. Verify that `p_in_base` equals `[0.0, 0.40, 0.10]` $\text{m}$ ($\pm 10^{-9}\text{ m}$) and $q(2.006\text{ s}) = 0.62\text{ rad}$ ($\pm 10^{-9}\text{ rad}$).

items.x: **If your result differs:** When $q_1 = \pi/2\text{ rad}$ and $q_2 = 0\text{ rad}$, both the $0.25\text{ m}$ `link_1` offset and the $0.15\text{ m}$ `tool0` offset point along the $+Y$ axis of `base_link` ($0.25 + 0.15 = 0.40\text{ m}$); and $\alpha = \frac{2.006 - 2.000}{0.010} = 0.60 \implies 0.50 + 0.60(0.20) = 0.62\text{ rad}$.

blocks.x: Graded package - the graph's promises and the arm's chain

[`exercises/06-robotics.T2.06a/`](../exercises/06-robotics.T2.06a/) turns this section into a test. `starter.py` holds seven holes: `qos_compatible` (two inequalities, not a match), `urdf_revolute_z`, `mat4_mul`, `transform_point`, `invert_rigid` (`R^T`, `-R^T p`), `interpolate` (refusing extrapolation the way tf2 does) and `topic_bandwidth_mb_s`. Edit it, then run the tests the way CI does:

The tests are behavioural: all **16** QoS combinations must match the `offered >= requested` rule, including the two that fail (Best-Effort into Reliable, Volatile into Transient Local); a zero joint must be a pure translation and a quarter turn must send $+X$ to $+Y$; two product orders must land the origin at **absolute** positions ($(0.1, 0.1)$ and $(0.2, 0)$), because comparing the two products to each other is symmetric and passes a reversed multiply; the rigid inverse must round-trip a point and undo a translation; a query outside the buffer must **raise**; and the bandwidth must scale with the subscriber count. The transfer suite builds the plant's own arm as a tf2 chain - `Rz(q1) Trans(L1) Rz(q2) Trans(L2)` from `plant.L1`/`plant.L2` - and requires it to reproduce `plant.fk` at five poses, to keep a tool point at the plant's own tip plus `d` along the tool axis, and to invert into the base seen from the tool at the tip's distance. Four planted faults - `qos_equality`, `joint_turns_backwards`, `product_reversed`, `interpolate_extrapolates` - each fail the test named for them.

items.x: **QoS is two inequalities, not a match.** Score Reliable $= 1$, Best-Effort $= 0$, Transient Local $= 1$ and Volatile $= 0$, then require *both* `offered >= requested`. Of the $16$ `(Reliability, Durability)` pairs, $9$ connect: the two that fail this exercise's eye are Best-Effort into Reliable and Volatile into Transient Local.

**One joint, then the chain.** `urdf_revolute_z(xyz, q)` is $\begin{bmatrix} R_z(q) & xyz \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, so a zero $q$ is pure translation and a quarter turn sends $+X$ to $+Y$. With $q_1 = \pi/2$ the $0.25\ \text{m}$ link offset itself lands at $[0, 0.25, 0]$, and the $0.15\ \text{m}$ tool offset is rotated by the *same* $R_z(\pi/2)$: $[0, 0.15, 0]$. Adding the $0.10\ \text{m}$ base height gives $[0, 0.40, 0.10]$.

**Interpolation is a fraction of the buffer.** $\alpha = (2.006 - 2.000)/(2.010 - 2.000) = 0.60$, so $q = 0.50 + 0.60(0.70 - 0.50) = 0.62\ \text{rad}$; a $t_{\text{query}}$ outside $[t_a, t_b]$ must raise, exactly as `tf2` throws `ExtrapolationException` instead of guessing.

**Bandwidth counts subscribers.** $R = N_{\text{sub}} B_{\text{msg}} f_{\text{pub}}/10^6$, so $2 \times 250{,}000 \times 60 = 30.0\ \text{MB/s}$ - a single-subscriber answer is short by exactly the subscriber count.

**What the suite refuses.** `interpolate` refuses a query outside the two samples' span: extrapolating is a different model, not a longer line, so it raises `ValueError` rather than inventing a value.

blocks.x: Inject the first row of the `## 8. Common mistakes` table: subscribe to the camera stream with the default `Reliable` profile while the publisher offers `Best-Effort`, keeping the worked example's $250{,}000\text{ B}$ frames at $60\text{ Hz}$ to two subscribers.

items.x: **Inject:** build the `/camera/depth` subscriber with `rclpy.qos.QoSProfile(depth=10, reliability=ReliabilityPolicy.RELIABLE)` instead of `SensorDataQoS()`.

**Symptom:** `ros2 topic list` shows the topic and the publisher reports $60\text{ Hz}$, which is $30\text{ MB/s}$ of offered traffic, yet the subscriber's callback never fires - $0$ messages, no exception, no timeout.

**Diagnose:** the publisher is running, so the transport, the domain id and the message type are all fine; `ros2 topic info -v` shows offered `BEST_EFFORT` against requested `RELIABLE`, and the rule fails on Reliability alone - durability matches, so it is not the `Volatile`/`Transient Local` row.
**Fix:** request `SensorDataQoS()` (Best-Effort) on the subscriber, and prove it by counting $60$ callbacks in one wall-clock second with `ros2 topic hz` reporting $60.000$.

Compute the total network data rate $R_{\text{MB/s}} = \frac{N_{\text{sub}} \cdot B_{\text{msg}} \cdot f_{\text{pub}}}{10^6}$ in $\text{MB/s}$ (tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}\text{ MB/s}$).

head: Symptom
Root cause
2-minute fix
rows: `ros2 topic echo` or subscriber node shows nothing even though `ros2 topic list` shows the topic exists
QoS incompatibility (`Best-Effort` sensor publisher vs `Reliable` subscriber, or `Volatile` publisher vs `Transient Local` subscriber) or mismatched `ROS_DOMAIN_ID`.
Run `ros2 topic info -v <topic>` to inspect offered vs. requested QoS policies and use `SensorDataQoS` (`Best-Effort`) when subscribing to camera/IMU streams.
Fast $100text{ Hz}$ timer freezes whenever a service callback or action server runs
Used the default `SingleThreadedExecutor` without `CallbackGroups`, so the long callback blocks the single thread.
Assign the slow callback to a separate `MutuallyExclusiveCallbackGroup` (or `ReentrantCallbackGroup`) and spin the node with a `MultiThreadedExecutor`.
`tf2::ExtrapolationException: Lookup would require extrapolation into the future`
Asked `tf2` for the transform at `now()` before `robot_state_publisher`'s latest message arrived, or clock skew exists between two machines.
Query `tf2::TimePointZero` for the latest available transform, or pass the sensor message's `header.stamp` with a short timeout (`50 ms`) and synchronize clocks via `chrony`/`PTP`.
`ros2_control` loop prints `Overrun detected!` every few seconds
Performed blocking socket/serial reads or dynamic memory allocation (`new`/`std::vector::push_back`) inside `read()` or `update()`.
Use non-blocking `O_NONBLOCK` SocketCAN / lock-free ring buffers in `read()` and pre-allocate all buffers inside `on_init()` / `on_configure()`.
